lesson.title: When a Whole Group of Atoms Acts Like One Ion
lesson.summary: A polyatomic ion is a tightly bonded cluster of atoms held together by covalent bonds that, as a complete unit, carries an overall electric charge and behaves exactly like a single ion in forming ionic compounds.
lesson.body:
So far, every ion in this chapter has been a single atom that gained or lost electrons, like Na+ or Cl-. Polyatomic ions break that pattern. A polyatomic ion is a group of two or more atoms bonded together by covalent bonds, the same electron-sharing bonds that hold together neutral molecules, except the group as a whole carries a leftover positive or negative charge because the total number of electrons in the group does not exactly match the total number of protons. That charged group then behaves as a single, indivisible unit whenever it participates in an ionic compound, moving around, packing into lattices, and balancing charge exactly the way a monatomic ion like Cl- does.

This is really a merger of two ideas already covered. The bonds inside the ion, say the four bonds inside a sulfate ion, are covalent bonds, formed by sharing electron pairs between nonmetal atoms. But the ion as a whole then forms an ionic compound with an oppositely charged partner ion through the same electrostatic attraction that holds together any ionic solid. A crystal of calcium carbonate, the mineral that makes up limestone and chalk, is a lattice of Ca2+ ions and CO3 2- ions, and inside every carbonate ion, one carbon atom is covalently bonded to three oxygen atoms, with the whole four-atom cluster carrying a 2- charge.

A handful of polyatomic ions show up constantly in chemistry and are worth knowing by formula and charge. Nitrate is NO3-, sulfate is SO4 2-, carbonate is CO3 2-, phosphate is PO4 3-, hydroxide is OH-, cyanide is CN-, and ammonium is NH4+, the one common polyatomic cation among a list otherwise dominated by anions. Related ions differ by one oxygen or one hydrogen: sulfite, SO3 2-, has one fewer oxygen than sulfate; nitrite, NO2-, has one fewer oxygen than nitrate; and bicarbonate, HCO3-, is carbonate with one extra hydrogen added, which also drops its charge from 2- to 1-.

Charge balancing with polyatomic ions works exactly like it does with monatomic ions, it just requires treating the whole polyatomic ion as one package. Ammonium sulfate, a common fertilizer, needs two ammonium ions, each contributing 1+, to balance the 2- charge on one sulfate ion, giving the formula (NH4)2SO4. The parentheses around NH4 signal that the subscript 2 applies to the entire ammonium ion, not just to one of its atoms, a formatting detail that becomes essential once formula writing and naming are covered in the next two sections.

Recognizing polyatomic ions on sight, rather than trying to figure out bonding from scratch every time, is a shortcut that pays off across the rest of ionic chemistry. Once a student can spot that MgSO4 contains Mg2+ and the intact sulfate ion, rather than four separate oxide ions and a sulfur atom, naming the compound, writing its formula from its name, and predicting its charge-balanced ratio with other ions all become far more manageable.
